facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period in western North America, shortly before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
facts.quote: It was among the last species of non-avian dinosaurs on Earth before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, which lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now western North America.

facts.statement: Fossils of Pachycephalosaurus have been found in Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Alberta.
facts.quote: Remains have been excavated in Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Alberta.

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus is known mainly from a single skull and thick skull roofs measuring 22 cm, with estimates of its length at 4.5 meters and weight between 370 and 450 kilograms.
facts.quote: Mainly known from a single skull and a few extremely thick skull roofs (at 22 cm thick), Pachycephalosaurus is estimated to have reached 4.5 m long and weighed 370 - 450 kg.

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus was a bipedal herbivore with long strong legs and small five-fingered hands.
facts.quote: Like other pachycephalosaurids, Pachycephalosaurus was a bipedal herbivore, possessing long, strong legs and somewhat small arms with five-fingered hands.

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus is the largest known pachycephalosaur, distinguished by an extremely thick, slightly domed skull roof.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurus is the largest-known pachycephalosaur, known for having an extremely thick, slightly domed skull roof

facts.statement: The skull structure suggests Pachycephalosaurus used its dome as a battering ram for defense or intraspecific combat, similar to modern bighorn sheep or muskoxen.
facts.quote: visually, the structure of the skull suggests a "battering ram" function in life, evolved for use as a defensive mechanism or intra-species combat, similar to what is seen with today's bighorn sheep or muskoxen

facts.statement: The hypothesis that Pachycephalosaurus used its skull dome for head-butting has been disputed in recent years.
facts.quote: This hypothesis has been disputed in recent years.

facts.statement: The genus Tylosteus is considered synonymous with Pachycephalosaurus.
facts.quote: The genus Tylosteus is synonymous with Pachycephalosaurus.

facts.statement: The synonymy of Stygimoloch with Pachycephalosaurus is disputed due to differences in the rock layers where their specimens were found.
facts.quote: The proposed synonymy for Stygimoloch with Pachycephalosaurus, however, has been disputed in recent literature due to temporal difference in the rock layers where specimens attributed to each genera have been recovered.

facts.statement: American paleontologist Joseph Leidy named the taxon Tylosteus ornatus seventy-one years before Pachycephalosaurus was described, based on a bone fragment he interpreted as reptile armor.
facts.quote: Seventy-one years prior to the description and naming of Pachycephalosaurus, American paleontologist Joseph Leidy named the new taxon Tylosteus ornatus for a bone fragment interpreted as the armor of a reptile.

facts.statement: Donald Baird and John R. Horner independently identified the Tylosteus holotype ANSP 8568 as a squamosal from a Pachycephalosaurus skull.
facts.quote: Baird and John R. Horner independently came across the Tylosteus holotype ANSP 8568 in the collections of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia and concluded that it was the squamosal from a skull of Pachycephalosaurus

facts.statement: In 1986, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature affirmed that Pachycephalosaurus is the valid name, while Tylosteus ornatus was rejected.
facts.quote: Baird advocated for conserving Pachycephalosaurus and rendering Tylosteus ornatus a nomen oblitum, which was affirmed by the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature in 1986 where Tylosteus was made a nomen rejectum and Pachycephalosaurus a nomen conservandum.

facts.statement: In 1990, W. P. Coombs suggested a tooth found by Hatcher came from a pachycephalosaurid, possibly Pachycephalosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1990, American paleontologist W. P. Coombs stated the tooth came from a pachycephalosaurid, possibly even Pachycephalosaurus itself.

facts.statement: A partial skull of Pachycephalosaurus was discovered in 1930 by George Fryer Sternberg in the Lance Formation of Niobrara County, Wyoming.
facts.quote: In 1930, American paleontologist George Fryer Sternberg discovered a partial skull within the Lance Formation of Niobrara County, Wyoming

facts.statement: The species Pachycephalosaurus wyomingensis was named by Charles W. Gilmore in 1931.
facts.quote: P. wyomingensis, the type and currently only valid species of Pachycephalosaurus, was named by Charles W. Gilmore in 1931

facts.statement: The genus Pachycephalosaurus was established in 1943 by Barnum Brown and Erich Maren Schlaikjer.
facts.quote: In 1943, Barnum Brown and Erich Maren Schlaikjer, with newer, more complete material, established the genus Pachycephalosaurus

facts.statement: Material attributable to Pachycephalosaurus was discovered in 2015 in the Scollard Formation of Alberta.
facts.quote: In 2015, some pachycephalosaurid material and a domed parietal attributable to Pachycephalosaurus were discovered in the Scollard Formation of Alberta

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus had a large bony dome on its skull up to 25 cm thick that cushioned its brain.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurus is famous for having a large, bony dome on top of its skull, up to 25 cm thick, which safely cushioned its brain

facts.statement: The bony spikes on the snout were likely blunted rather than sharp.
facts.quote: The spikes were probably blunted, not sharp

facts.quote: The skull was short and possessed large, rounded eye sockets that faced forward, suggesting that the animal had binocular vision

facts.statement: The animal had a small muzzle ending in a pointed beak.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurus had a small muzzle that ended in a pointed beak

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus had tiny teeth with leaf-shaped crowns.
facts.quote: The teeth were tiny, with leaf-shaped crowns

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur and possibly the largest of all pachycephalosaurids.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurus was bipedal and possibly the largest of all pachycephalosaurids

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus was estimated to be about 4.5 meters long and weigh between 370 and 450 kilograms.
facts.quote: It has been estimated that Pachycephalosaurus was about 4.5 m long and weighed about 370-450 kg

facts.statement: Younger individuals of Pachycephalosaurus may have had flatter skulls with larger horns projecting from the back.
facts.quote: Younger individuals of Pachycephalosaurus might have had flatter skulls and larger horns projecting from the back of the skull

facts.statement: As Pachycephalosaurus grew, its horns shrank and rounded while the dome expanded.
facts.quote: As the animal grew, the horns shrunk and rounded out as the dome grew

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus names the clade Pachycephalosauria, a group of herbivorous ornithischian dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of North America and Asia.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurus gives its name to Pachycephalosauria, a clade of herbivorous ornithischian dinosaurs that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in North America and Asia

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurs belonged to the clade Marginocephalia and were likely more closely related to ceratopsians than to ornithopods.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurs were a part of Marginocephalia, thus being likely more closely related to the ceratopsians than the ornithopods

facts.statement: In 2009, Horenr and Goodwin proposed that Stygimoloch and Dracorex are juvenile growth stages of Pachycephalosaurus and should be classified as synonyms.
facts.quote: In 2009, Horenr and Goodwin proposed that Stygimoloch and Dracorex represent younger growth stages of Pachycephalosaurus, and thus should be classified as junior synonyms

facts.statement: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul suggested that Stygimoloch might be a distinct species, P. spinifer, rather than just a growth stage of Pachycephalosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul proposed that, while Stygimoloch and Dracorex possibly represent different growth stages of Pachycephalosaurus, Stygimoloch might represent a different species, P. spinifer

facts.statement: A 2021 analysis by Evans and colleagues accepted Stygimoloch as a valid genus but agreed that Dracorex is a growth stage of either Stygimoloch or Pachycephalosaurus.
facts.quote: A 2021 phylogenetic analysis by Evans and colleagues accepted the validity of the genus Stygimoloch based on the same reason as Fowler (2017), but agreed with the consensus that Dracorex represents an ontogimorph of either Stygimoloch or Pachycephalosaurus instead of a distinct taxon

facts.statement: In 2025, Wroblewski treated Stygimoloch as a separate genus restricted to the uppermost Maastrichtian but agreed that Dracorex is morphologically identical to it or Pachycephalosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2025, Wroblewski treated Stygimoloch as a separate genus to which he attributed three specimens from the Ferris Formation, providing further evidence that this taxon was restricted to the uppermost Maastrichtian, but agreed with the consensus that Dracorex is morphologically identical to Stygimoloch (or Pachycephalosaurus)

facts.statement: In 2007, researchers proposed that related genera Stygimoloch and Dracorex were juvenile or female forms of Pachycephalosaurus.
facts.quote: However, in 2007, they were proposed to be juvenile or female morphologies of Pachycephalosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2009, Horner and Goodwin published findings showing that skull bones of Pachycephalosaurus and related forms exhibit extreme plasticity during growth.
facts.quote: Horner and M.B. Goodwin published their findings in 2009, showing that the spike and skull dome bones of all three "species" exhibit extreme plasticity

facts.statement: In 2016, baby skulls assigned to Pachycephalosaurus were described from the Hell Creek Formation, supporting the hypothesis that related flat-headed forms were juveniles.
facts.quote: The discovery of baby skulls assigned to Pachycephalosaurus that were described in 2016 from two different bone beds in the Hell Creek Formation has been presented as further evidence for this hypothesis.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Pachycephalosaurus used its dome for head-butting like bighorn sheep or for flank-butting like kangaroos.
facts.quote: It has been widely hypothesized for decades that Pachycephalosaurus and its relatives were the ancient, bipedal equivalents of bighorn sheep or musk oxen, where male individuals would ram each other headlong

facts.statement: A 2012 study suggested that cranial pathologies in a Pachycephalosaurus specimen were caused by aggressive behavior.
facts.quote: In 2012, a study showed that cranial pathologies in a P. wyomingensis specimen were likely due to agonistic behavior.

facts.statement: A 2013 study found that 22% of examined pachycephalosaur domes had lesions consistent with osteomyelitis, supporting the use of domes in combat.
facts.quote: Peterson et al. (2013) studied cranial pathologies among Pachycephalosauridae and found that 22% of all domes examined had lesions that are consistent with osteomyelitis

facts.statement: Histological examination reveals that pachycephalosaurid domes are made of fibrolamellar bone containing fibroblasts critical for wound healing.
facts.quote: Histological examination reveals that pachycephalosaurid domes are composed of a unique form of fibrolamellar bone that contains fibroblasts, which play a critical role in wound healing

facts.statement: Research by Cary Woodruff noted that the spine, pelvis, and tail of Pachycephalosaurus resemble those of kangaroos rather than head-butting animals.
facts.quote: Research headed by paleontologist Cary Woodruff noted that Pachycephalosaurus's spine, pelvis and tail share resemblances to kangaroos over headbutting animals like bighorn sheep.

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus had very small, ridged teeth that were ineffective for chewing tough, fibrous plants.
facts.quote: Having very small, ridged teeth, they could not have chewed tough, fibrous plants like flowering shrubs as effectively as other dinosaurs of the same period.

facts.statement: The most complete fossil jaw of Pachycephalosaurus shows serrated, blade-like front teeth reminiscent of carnivorous theropods.
facts.quote: The most complete fossil jaw shows that it had serrated blade-like front teeth, reminiscent of those of carnivorous theropods.

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurus coexisted with diverse dinosaurs including ceratopsians, ankylosaurids, nodosaurids, and theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Other dinosaurs that shared its time and place include Thescelosaurus, the hadrosaurid Edmontosaurus and possibly Parasaurolophus, ceratopsians like Triceratops, Torosaurus, Nedoceratops, Tatankaceratops, and Leptoceratops, the ankylosaurid Ankylosaurus, the nodosaurids Denversaurus and Edmontonia, and the theropods Acheroraptor, Dakotaraptor, Ornithomimus, Struthiomimus, Anzu, Leptorhynchos, Pectinodon, Paronychodon, Richardoestesia, Nanotyrannus, and Tyrannosaurus.
